query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Using spark plasma sintering (SPS) to consolidate cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder limits chemical segregation, residual stress, and defect formation, thereby improving the alloy’s mechanical integrity compared to samples produced by conventional routes.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi alloy as mechanically alloyed, pre-alloyed powder with potential elemental inhomogeneities and high defect density from conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Apply rapid consolidation via spark plasma sintering (SPS) with controlled high heating rates and applied pressure.
generation.conditions: SPS processing in a vacuum or inert atmosphere with heating rates on the order of 100 °C/min, a short dwell time (several minutes), and moderate pressure; subsequent mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and hardness tests) at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, nearly fully dense microstructure with reduced grain boundary segregation and lower residual stress.
generation.mechanism: The rapid heating and short hold time in SPS minimizes time for diffusion-driven segregation and reduces residual stress buildup, while applied pressure enhances densification and uniform elemental distribution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventionally processed samples (casting or slower additive manufacturing), the SPS-consolidated alloy is expected to show increased yield strength and hardness with less microstructural inhomogeneity and lower defect density.
generation.baseline: Conventionally fabricated cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi parts produced via casting or standard additive manufacturing methods.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is valid for powder feedstock processed under SPS conditions optimized to avoid unwanted phase transformations; it applies primarily to laboratory-scale consolidation where thermal gradients and pressure can be accurately controlled.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in mechanical properties is uncertain and likely sensitive to the precise SPS parameters chosen; further experimental tuning is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder: one group consolidated via spark plasma sintering under the specified rapid processing conditions, and a control group processed using conventional methods (e.g., casting or standard LAM). Carry out detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM, EDS, and XRD for residual stress) and mechanical testing (tensile strength, hardness measurements).
measurements: Grain size and phase uniformity (via microscopy and EDS mapping)
Residual stress levels (using X-ray diffraction techniques)
Mechanical performance metrics (yield strength, tensile strength, hardness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-processed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in mechanical properties, reduced residual stresses, and lower segregation/defect levels compared to the control group, or if they display unexpected new defects, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Since 2004, when Yeh et al. [] and Cantor et al. [] published the results of multicomponent equiatomic alloys, eventually called high-entropy alloys (HEAs), combinations of many components have been developed due to their improved properties compared to classic alloys (of a main element with more than 50 at.%). Yeh et al. defined these alloys as containing a minimum of five components that account for between 5% and 35% by atomic weight. Cantor was the first to create an equiatomic alloy from the CoCrFeMnNi system, and it was observed that the mechanical characteristics of high-entropy alloys rely on chemical composition and microstructure [,]. If certain thermomechanical treatments are applied to this alloy, its mechanical properties can be considerably improved. For example, after treatment, the yield strength reaches up to 1834 MPa and the ultimate tensile strength rises to 2069 MPa, with uniform elongation of 1.4% and total elongation of 7.4% at room temperature. This alloy has high fracture resistance and low-temperature ductility, although there have been only few investigations on how it react to corrosion. The addition of Zr to multielement alloys allows the improvement of some mechanical properties []; thus, in TiMoNbZrx alloy, Zr determined the improvement of wear resistance, due to the formation of an oxide film that acts as a lubricant []. In terms of corrosion resistance, grain refinement plays a great role, and a small addition of Zr can contribute to grain refinement []. Thus, our study focuses on the use of the Mo and Zr in an HEA for the manufacture of mechanical parts used in the geothermal industry at high temperature and in corrosive media. The impact of Zr addition on the CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy’s microstructure, elastic modulus, and corrosion characteristics is examined in this work. In order to analyze the microstructure of the samples with and without Zr, optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) are employed, microhardness tests are performed, a three-point bending test is used to evaluate the modulus of elasticity and linear polarization (LP), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is applied to examine electrochemical responses, corrosion kinetics, and interface parameters.

This paper focuses on the microstructure, phase composition, mechanical, tribological and corrosion properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the CoCrCuFeNi system depending on copper content, which was varied from 0 to 20 at. % with an increment of 5%. CoCrCuFeNi alloys were manufactured by powder metallurgy methods: mechanical alloying and hot pressing of element mixtures. The solubility limit of copper in CoCrFeNi solid solution was found to be 9 at. %. Segregation of irregularly shaped copper grains sized 1–30 μm is observed at concentrations above this solubility limit. As copper concentration increases, the phase composition of CoCrCuFeNi alloys changes from the single phase based on FCC1 solid solution (Cu = 0–5 at. %) to the dual-phase FCC1 + FCC2 alloy (Cu = 10–20 at. %), where FCC1 is the main phase and FCC2 is the secondary copper-rich phase. Tribological tests have shown that doping the CoCrFeNi alloy with copper increased wear resistance by 23% due to solid solution hardening.
